text: 4. Evaluation EdgeAgent builds upon Apple’s native MLX runtime, fundamentally restructuring its underlying C++ graph executor to enable zero-copy UMA memory management. Furthermore, it introduces lightweight cross-layer APIs to synchronize multi-agent execution states such as variance in drafting difficulty and tool-induced stalls with the underlying scheduler. We comprehensively evaluate EdgeAgent using trace-driven multi-agent workflows to demonstrate its end-to-end makespan, concurrent throughput, and resilience to tool-induced execution stalls. 4.1. Experimental Setup Hardware Testbed. Primary experiments are conducted on an Apple M4 SoC equipped with 32 GB of unified memory and a 120 GB/s UMA bus. The SoC integrates a 10-core CPU (4 performance + 6 efficiency) with the ARMv9 SME2 extension, alongside a 10-core GPU. To verify EdgeAgent ’s generalization, the key ablations are additionally evaluated on an Apple M4 Pro SoC with 64 GB of unified memory and a 273 GB/s UMA bus, whose 14-core CPU (10 performance + 4 efficiency) and 20-core GPU shift the compute-to-bandwidth balance relative to the base M4. Since both SoCs share the SME2 extension, the M4 Pro isolates the effect of the bandwidth balance rather than the micro-kernel backend. Together they exemplify the stringent memory-bandwidth and computational constraints of modern edge AI environments. Models. We evaluate our system using two representative large language models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) , a reasoning-focused model that exhibits severe drafting difficulty (yielding low acceptance rates) during its extensive chain-of-thought (CoT) generation, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Llama Team, 2024 ) for standard instruction-following workloads. For configurations involving speculative decoding, we uniformly adopt EAGLE-3 ( Li et al., 2025d ) , a state-of-the-art draft generation and verification framework. All models and tensor operations are executed in FP16 precision. Datasets and Workloads. Lacking deterministic multi-agent benchmarks for rigorous micro-architectural evaluation, we construct a workload-representative trace synthesizer. We first sample real-world prompts to build a heterogeneous workload pool across three distinct agent domains, whose profiling characteristics are summarized in Table 2 : • Reasoning Task (LongBench ( Bai et al., 2025 ) ): Features hard-to-draft logical reasoning, such as orchestrator making decisions and reading comprehension summaries. • Structured Output Task (MBPP ( Austin et al., 2021 ) ): Comprises programming tasks that generate structured, highly predictable code sequences. • Tool Execution Task (ToolBench ( Guo et al., 2024 ) ): Provides tool-use and API invocation prompts, representing the interactive behaviors of autonomous agents. To construct the synthetic trace, our workload generator applies three steps. First, we blend the sampled prompts in a 1:2:2 ratio (Reasoning : Code : Tool). This reflects the structure of real agent systems, where a reasoning orchestrator is outnumbered by code- and tool-executing workers. It also avoids the degenerate reasoning-heavy regime: reasoning agents accept few tokens per verification step and therefore take many steps, so a 1:1:1 mix ends in a long tail in which a single reasoning agent drains the queue alone, the speculative batch is under-filled, and no scheduling headroom remains for HAL to redistribute. Second, we inject log-uniform stochastic pauses into tool-use requests to simulate API latencies. Finally, to evaluate realistic scheduling and makespan, requests are dispatched via a Poisson process with intra-agent delays; conversely, peak throughput measurements bypass these arrival delays to maintain continuous system saturation. To systematically isolate our performance contributions, we evaluate EdgeAgent against three baseline configurations, all executed strictly on the GPU to represent standard state-of-the-practice deployments: • Batch-AR: Vanilla non-speculative baselines for naive continuous batching. • Seq-SD (EAGLE-3): State-of-the-art single-stream speculative decoding. It establishes the isolated single-agent performance bound. • Batch-SD (Batched EAGLE-3): The strongest concurrent baseline, utilizing GPU-bound continuous batching with a fixed per-request draft budget ( L i = 16 L_{i}=16 ). It highlights two critical flaws of standard scheduling: computational waste from static draft lengths, and severe compute stalling during agent tool execution. Metrics. We evaluate overall performance across two primary dimensions: user-centric latency and system-centric throughput. To capture the actual user-perceived turnaround time, we first measure the end-to-end makespan, defined as the total wall-clock time required to complete the hybrid workload. Complementarily, the system throughput is measured by global throughput, the aggregate token generation rate across all concurrent streams. 4.2. End-to-End Evaluation Figure 7 . To evaluate the overall makespan and global throughput of EdgeAgent , we construct a spectrum of concurrent workloads. As illustrated in Figure 7 , we progressively inject task heterogeneity and external tool-induced stalls to expose the scheduling bottlenecks of existing frameworks. This evaluation isolates the end-to-end efficiency of the system, while the specific micro-architectural mechanisms driving these results are analyzed in the subsequent subsections (§ 4.3 –§ 4.5 ). Baseline Inference Performance. We first establish the baseline performance using a continuous, pure code-generation workload without tool-induced stalls (Figures 7 (a) and 7 (e)). At N = 4 N=4 , where N N denotes the number of actively decoding agents in the system, EdgeAgent achieves a global throughput of 33.6 tok/s (DeepSeek) and 28.0 tok/s (LLaMA). These metrics represent 1.29 × 1.29\times speedups over the optimized Batch-SD baseline. This gain reflects our UMA-aware execution layer, which combines the optimized SME kernels with zero-copy TP, prior to enabling HAL scheduling and stall-aware context switching. Component ablation. To isolate each contribution, we enable EdgeAgent’s optimizations incrementally on top of the Batch-SD baseline: first the optimized SME kernels, then zero-copy TP, and finally HAL scheduling, measuring the end-to-end makespan for 2, 3, and 4 concurrent agents on both the M4 and the M4 Pro (Figure 8 ). Each step reduces the makespan. Together, the optimized SME kernels and zero-copy TP constitute our UMA-aware execution layer, which achieves up to a 1.29 × 1.29\times speedup over Batch-SD. Enabling HAL scheduling provides an additional 1.05 1.05 – 1.17 × 1.17\times improvement over the corresponding UMA-aware configuration. Offline packing is included in every bar and is small: 13–16 s on the M4 and 6.2 s on the M4 Pro, under 5 % 5\% of the makespan. Adaptability to Mixed Workload. To evaluate scheduling efficiency under varying sequence predictability, we introduce a mixed workload combining reasoning and coding tasks without tool-induced stalls (Figures 7 (b) and 7 (f)). While the overall throughput naturally decreases across all systems due to the hard-to-draft reasoning steps, a static draft-length allocation ( L = 16 L=16 ) wastes compute resources generating and verifying unaccepted tokens during low-acceptance reasoning phases. By utilizing dynamic budgeting (§ 4.4 ), EdgeAgent mitigates this overhead and achieves a 1.33 × \times speedup over the Batch-SD baseline , demonstrating the efficiency of predictability-aware resource allocation. Sensitivity to Workload Composition. To test whether the 1:2:2 default mix flatters our results, we sweep the reasoning/code/tool ratio from 1:1:1 to 1:4:4 while holding the arrival process and concurrency settings fixed. HAL scheduling improves on the fixed-budget baseline across the entire sweep, and its gain grows monotonically as the mix shifts toward structured code and tool generation (Figure 9 ). This is the expected direction: structured-output agents are highly predictable and a static L = 16 L=16 budget caps the tokens they could otherwise accept, whereas extra budget spent on reasoning-heavy agents is largely wasted on rejected drafts. The 1:2:2 default therefore sits at an interior and conservative operating point of this curve, not a favorable peak. Adaptability to Tool Stalls. Real-world agent workflows frequently stall during external tool invocations. To simulate this, we inject log-uniform tool-execution stall durations of [ 1 , 10 ] [1,10] seconds and [ 1,100 ] [1,100] seconds into the mixed workload (Figures 7 (c)-(d) and 7 (g)-(h)). Under the extreme [ 1,100 ] [1,100] s stall configuration at N = 4 N=4 (Figure 7 d), head-of-line blocking in Batch-SD severely delays execution, inflating its makespan to 213.1 seconds (DeepSeek). In contrast, EdgeAgent leverages its asynchronous suspend-and-yield mechanism (§ 4.5 ) to evict stalled agents and reclaim verification slots. This effectively hides the stall, compressing the total makespan to just 120.6 seconds and delivering a 1.77 × \times speedup over the optimized Batch-SD baseline. Overall Performance Scaling. Across the evaluated configurations, our UMA-aware execution layer, which combines the optimized SME kernels with zero-copy TP, achieves up to a 1.29 × 1.29\times speedup over Batch-SD. The primary systemic gains emerge in stall-intensive environments, where the complete EdgeAgent system reaches a 1.77 × 1.77\times speedup by combining UMA-aware execution, HAL scheduling, and stall-aware context switching. Furthermore, scaling concurrency from N = 2 N=2 to N = 4 N=4 consistently widens this margin, indicating that the system effectively utilizes edge UMA resources under highly irregular execution patterns. 4.3. The SME kernel consistently approaches the hardware’s theoretical peak of ∼ \sim 2.3 TFLOPS. The foundational execution engine of EdgeAgent is built upon our architecture-aware heterogeneous tensor parallelism. This section systematically dissects how the framework maximizes the absolute compute capacity of the UMA architecture while mitigating the synchronization overhead typically associated with cross-device execution. We begin by quantifying the macroscopic throughput and latency improvements achieved during the compute-bound prefill phase. Following this, a rigorous latency decomposition demonstrates the elimination of tensor aggregation overhead via our zero-copy synchronization computation graph. The evaluation concludes by isolating the micro-architectural efficiency of our custom SME kernel, confirming its capacity to sustain hardware-saturating utilization across highly skewed inference workloads. 4.3.1. Accelerating Compute-Bound Prefill To evaluate the prefill performance of our heterogeneous tensor parallelism, we adopt two metrics. The primary latency metric is time to first token (TTFT), which measures the end-to-end duration required to process the input prompt and generate the initial token. To quantify overall system capacity, we measure prefill throughput, defined as the number of prompt tokens processed per second. They demonstrate the efficiency of our CPU-GPU co-execution under large contextual workloads, or rather the compute-bound workload. The results presented in Figure 10 confirm the compute-bound nature of the prefill phase, where standalone GPU and CPU executions remain stable at 232 and 132 tokens per second. By leveraging heterogeneous tensor parallelism, our system effectively surpasses these isolated hardware ceilings. At a prompt length of 1024, the co-execution engine achieves a peak throughput of 304.5 tokens per second, yielding a 1.31 × \times speedup over the GPU-only baseline. This compute expansion directly translates to latency improvements for extended contexts. For a 4096 token prompt, our system reduces the TTFT from 21.0 seconds on the standalone GPU to 16.2 seconds. These measurements demonstrate that our architecture successfully aggregates physical compute units without triggering shared memory bus contention during dense matrix operations. 4.3.2. Zero-Copy Synchronization Standard UMA co-execution relies on explicit tensor concatenation Concat , triggering expensive 𝒪 ⁡ ( M ⋅ N ) \mathcal{O}(M\cdot N) memory copies that bottleneck the shared bus. EdgeAgent eliminates this via a zero-copy computation graph, pre-allocating a single memory block for in-place, simultaneous writes and reducing aggregation to a lightweight barrier. Figure 11 decomposes the end-to-end latency. In the memory-bound decode phase ( M ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 } M\in\{1,4,16\} ), baseline memory copies ( Concat ) inflate the sub-millisecond pure compute time by >50%. EdgeAgent ’s zero-copy architecture eliminates this bottleneck, yielding a consistent ∼ \sim 1.14 × \times speedup. At micro-batch M = 128 M=128 , the overhead remains severe (+0.90 ms on top of ∼ \sim 2.8 ms compute), which EdgeAgent compresses to just +0.04 ms, delivering a 1.31 × \times speedup. Conversely, during massive prefill ( M = 1024 M=1024 ), the dense 𝒪 ⁡ ( M ⋅ K ⋅ N ) \mathcal{O}(M\cdot K\cdot N) compute surges past 20 ms, naturally amortizing the 𝒪 ⁡ ( M ⋅ N ) \mathcal{O}(M\cdot N) synchronization overhead to < 3 % <3\% . This confirms that EdgeAgent introduces negligible synchronization delays across all batch scales. 4.3.3. Custom SME Kernel efficiency To maximize CPU utilization during co-execution, relying on general-purpose libraries like Apple’s BNNS is suboptimal for the highly skewed tensor shapes of LLM inference. We address this by implementing a custom GEMM kernel strictly optimized for ARM’s SME. Unlike stateless BLAS libraries that redundantly repack static weights upon invocation, our kernel pre-packs model weights offline during initialization. This eliminates data-layout transformation overheads from the runtime critical path. We evaluate our kernel against BNNS on standard MLP projections, specifically the 4096 × 14336 4096\times 14336 up-projection and the 14336 × 4096 14336\times 4096 down-projection. Measuring pure online inference throughput exclusive of offline packing time, the empirical results presented in Figure 12 demonstrate major architectural advantages across both decoding and prefill regimes. During autoregressive decoding for M ≤ 16 M\leq 16 , BNNS suffers from significant dispatch overheads. For a batch size of M = 1 M=1 on the down-projection layer, BNNS yields only 19.0 GFLOPS. By circumventing these framework overheads, our custom kernel delivers 85.0 GFLOPS, achieving a 4.47 × \times speedup. Conversely, under massive prefill workloads for M ≥ 2048 M\geq 2048 , BNNS exhibits severe throughput degradation, dropping to 639.3 GFLOPS on the down-projection at M = 4096 M=4096 .
